blocks.heading: Informing, persuading and reminding
blocks.text:
An advertising purpose is the intended effect on the audience. Informing supplies useful information, such as a product's availability, price, location, features or conditions. Persuading tries to influence preference and encourage a choice. Reminding keeps an existing product or organisation in people's awareness. These purposes can overlap. A message giving a new service's location may also use a clear image or claim to encourage customers to prefer it. Identify the relevant parts of the message instead of assuming the whole communication has a single possible role.

A refill shop might publish its opening hours and explain which containers customers can bring. That reduces uncertainty about how to use the service. If it also emphasises convenience to encourage a switch from another shopping habit, it has a persuasive element. A repeated short reminder before the weekend may aim to keep the shop in mind. Different purposes call for different evidence of success. Awareness might be checked through whether people know the location, while a purchase objective requires evidence about customer action. A large number of views alone does not prove a sales objective was met. The intended effect and the observed result should therefore be stated separately.

blocks.heading: Methods and audience fit
blocks.text:
An advertising method is the communication channel used to reach an audience. Common methods include printed notices or newspapers, radio, outdoor signs and digital media. Print can carry detailed information that a reader can revisit, but requires access and attention. Radio can reach listeners over an area and use spoken explanation, but a brief message may be missed or forgotten. Outdoor signs can reach people passing a particular location; their usefulness depends on where they are displayed and whether the message can be read in time. Digital methods can combine images, text and contact opportunities, while depending on suitable access.

For a local bicycle-maintenance service, a large audience outside its service area may be less useful than a smaller relevant audience nearby. A detailed digital notice could explain repair options, while a sign near the workshop could help residents find it. Repeating an unclear message does not resolve missing information. The business should match the channel's format to what customers need to know and compare cost with the likely relevant reach. Do not assume that a free posting has no opportunity cost: preparation and responding to enquiries use time, even where no placement fee is charged. Nor does paying for a large campaign guarantee that people will notice or believe it.

Common methods are television, radio, newspapers and magazines, billboards and posters, leaflets, websites and social media, sponsorship of events or teams, and displays at the point of sale. Firms advertise to launch a new product, increase sales and market share, build brand loyalty, compete with rivals, and inform customers of price changes or special offers. Governments also advertise to inform the public, for example in health campaigns.

blocks.heading: A justified method choice
blocks.text: Choose a method by linking an audience characteristic to a channel feature and then to the intended effect. If customers need to see dimensions or appearance, a visual format may help. If connectivity is unreliable, digital communication alone may leave some people uninformed. These explanations connect the method to the purpose rather than listing media without reasons. A combination can be appropriate if each channel serves a distinct audience or information need at an acceptable cost. A radio announcement can suit a spoken location reminder, while a leaflet can retain detailed dimensions for later reading. State which information the audience needs before comparing these methods; neither example establishes a universal ranking.
